title: DeepMind AI Agents Now Control Gemini Experiment Compute
summary: Google DeepMind VP Koray Kavukcuoglu confirms AI agents now control part of the lab's compute budget to run experiments for upcoming Gemini models.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Google DeepMind AI agents now autonomously control part of the lab's compute budget to run experiments for upcoming Gemini models.
- DeepMind does not reward agent chain-of-thought during training, keeping intentions reviewable in natural language before execution.
- Research VP Koray Kavukcuoglu said full recursive self-improvement remains far off, and the exact compute share controlled by agents was not disclosed.


Google DeepMind has crossed a significant operational threshold: AI agents now autonomously control part of the lab's[compute budget](https://emergent.sh/glossary/compute-budget) to run experiments for upcoming Gemini models. Research VP Koray Kavukcuoglu disclosed the milestone on November 25, 2026, during a company podcast, marking one of the first confirmed cases of a leading AI lab delegating resource allocation to its own systems. Officially launched on November 25, 2026, the approach represents a step toward agentic research infrastructure, though Kavukcuoglu stressed that full recursive self-improvement remains far off.


## How DeepMind Agents Control Compute


Kavukcuoglu confirmed that agents at DeepMind now decide how to allocate a portion of the lab's compute resources for experimentation on future Gemini iterations. The agents select which experiments to run, manage resource budgets, and execute workflows without human intervention for each step. The lab did not quantify what share of total compute the agents control, nor did it specify which types of experiments fall under agentic oversight. The disclosure suggests DeepMind is moving beyond static research pipelines toward systems that dynamically optimize their own development cycles.


This operational shift is distinct from broader discussions of agent capabilities in consumer products. DeepMind's agents operate within the lab's internal infrastructure, optimizing research workflows rather than interacting with end users or external environments. The focus is on accelerating model development by offloading experiment design and resource management to trained agents.


## Chain-of-Thought Transparency as a Safety Mechanism


A critical safety guardrail underpins the system. During training, DeepMind does not reward an agent's internal chain-of-thought. Kavukcuoglu explained that this design choice ensures agent intentions remain unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they execute actions. By withholding rewards tied to reasoning steps, the lab preserves human oversight of agent decision-making processes.


The approach addresses a core challenge in agentic systems: opaque reasoning. If agents learn to optimize their internal thought processes for rewards, those processes may become inscrutable or misaligned with human reviewers' ability to verify intent. DeepMind's method keeps the reasoning layer transparent and legible, allowing researchers to audit agent plans before compute resources are committed. Kavukcuoglu did not describe how the lab balances this constraint with agent performance, or whether the transparency requirement limits the complexity of experiments agents can design.


## Recursive Self-Improvement Still Far Off


Kavukcuoglu drew a clear line between current capabilities and full recursive self-improvement, the scenario in which models continuously upgrade themselves in a closed loop. He stated that such a milestone is still far off, though he did not define a timeline or technical barriers. The distinction matters: today's agents allocate compute and run predefined experiment types, but they do not yet redesign core training algorithms, rewrite their own architectures, or autonomously discover novel learning paradigms.


The gap between resource management and recursive improvement is substantial. Resource allocation is a constrained optimization problem with clear metrics and boundaries. Recursive self-improvement requires agents to reason about their own learning processes, propose architectural changes, and validate improvements without human-defined success criteria. Kavukcuoglu's comments suggest DeepMind views the current system as a step toward, but not a realization of, that endpoint.


## Organizational Shift Toward General-Purpose Algorithms


Kavukcuoglu also described a broader restructuring within DeepMind. The lab is moving away from specialized teams like the one behind AlphaFold, toward what he called one general-purpose algorithm for science and products. Each Gemini generation is hand-built rather than fitted to a fixed architecture, a design philosophy that prioritizes flexibility over standardization.


He distinguished between visual accuracy and understanding in current models. Today's systems can depict physical processes, including fluid flows and collisions, with visual accuracy, he said, without grasping the underlying mechanics. On AGI, Kavukcuoglu avoided benchmark-driven definitions entirely, framing the milestone as the arrival of useful everyday products that people trust enough to hand decisions over to, as they might when working with another person.


## What This Means


DeepMind's deployment of agents to control compute represents a tangible shift in how leading labs operate. By delegating experiment management to trained systems, the lab is testing whether agentic infrastructure can accelerate research cycles without sacrificing oversight. The chain-of-thought transparency mechanism is a notable safety design, though its long-term scalability remains an open question. Kavukcuoglu's cautious framing around recursive self-improvement suggests DeepMind is aware of the gap between current capabilities and the sci-fi endpoint often cited in AI discourse. For practitioners and researchers, the development signals that agentic workflows are moving from theoretical frameworks into production research environments, with real compute budgets and real experimental outcomes at stake.
